# Human-machine interface in smart factory: A systematic literature review

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Naveen Kumar, Seul Chan Lee

Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering/Engineering Research Institute, Gyeongsang National University, Jinju, Republic of Korea

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Smart factory Industry 4.0 Human-machine interface, Human factors Human-computer interaction Human operator

## A B S T R A C T

A smart factory is a form of manufacturing in the era of Industry 4.0 that has adopted new integrated manufacturing technologies. The importance of human–machine interfaces (HMIs) has been increasing due to the complexity of the current manufacturing context. Therefore, it is necessary to identify and understand HMIs in smart factories from a holistic perspective, which enables us to understand the overall picture. In this study, we conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) of HMIs to identify smart factory functions, tasks, information types, interaction modalities, and their impact on human operators from the perspectives of human factors and human–computer interaction. Seventy-seven articles were selected for SLR and analysed based on three research questions. We found four smart factory functions (operation and supervision, management, maintenance service, and cybersecurity) consisting of 18 tasks, including subtasks and functions. The effects of these functions, tasks, and HMIs on human operators are also discussed. Five interaction modalities (gaze, voice, gesture, tactile, and haptic) were used to perform these functions and tasks. This paper also discusses the practical use context of HMIs in smart factories and offers HMI recommendations for users, designers, and researchers. These findings provide insights into the design of HMIs in smart factories.

## 1. Introduction

The recent industrial revolution in the manufacturing world is known as Industry 4.0. This is the fourth industrial revolution based on the concept of ubiquitous computing in the manufacturing industry (Vaidya et al., 2018). A smart factory is a representative form of manufacturing in the era of Industry 4.0, which adopted new integrated manufacturing technologies, such as cyber manufacturing systems, augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and Internet of Things (IoT) (Xu et al., 2014). Cyber-physical production systems (CPPSs) in smart factories are expected to have reduced physical work, and operators will be involved more in cognitive work (Monostori et al., 2016). Accordingly, Cohen et al. (2018) reported that the role of human operators in future manufacturing sites will be shifted into decision-making actions, information interpretation, and observation of real-time sensor data.

In the manufacturing context, changes in work and sub-tasks have brought a paradigm shift in human-machine interfaces (HMIs) (Adwernat et al., 2020; Lucke et al., 2008; Monostori et al., 2016). In every industrial revolution, new information types and interactions in HMIs have been observed (Alc´acer and Cruz-Machado, 2019; Gorecky et al., 2014), such as batch interface (BI), command-line interface (CLI), text-based interface (TBI), graphical user interface (GUI), and natural user interface (NUI). Such different HMIs include different presentation methods, interactions, and information types according to changes in the industry. However, although the manufacturing industry attempts to progress towards the next version with the fourth industrial revolution, little attention has been paid to investigating HMIs in smart factories from the perspective of Human Factors and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) (Gorecky et al., 2014; Papcun et al., 2018).

To bridge this knowledge gap, in this study, we aimed to investigate the characteristics of HMIs in smart factories to provide a deeper understanding of them. Consequently, a systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted using the research framework depicted in Fig. 1. We considered two major parts of the smart factory: smart factory system (function, task, and information) and HMI (user interface and interaction), which primarily impact human operators from physical and cognitive perspectives. Accordingly, we elicited three research questions (RQs): (1) What types of functions, tasks, and information are used in smart factories? (2) What interaction modalities are used for HMI in smart factories? (3) How does the system and HMI impact human operators in a smart factory? All the concepts and terms, including functions, tasks, information types, and interaction, used in this study were investigated from the perspectives of Human Factors and HCI, rather than technological development. In the remainder of this paper, we first review related studies to understand the characteristics of HMIs based on industrial changes. We then explain how we applied the SLR method to answer the RQs. Subsequently, we discuss the results, discussions, and conclusions of this study.

## 2. Literature review

A literature review was conducted to understand HMIs in terms of the manufacturing industry. Researchers have defined HMIs in different ways (Vaidya et al., 2018; Zuehlke, 2010). HMI is defined as an interface that allows humans to interact with machines and systems (Papcun et al., 2018). Therefore, HMIs usually comprise two main interface elements: display and control. The display element can present the machine parameters, status of the machines, and process information, whereas control elements are used to provide input to the machines (Zhang, 2010).

HMIs evolve and change in the manufacturing sector according to the industrial revolution (Meixner et al., 2010). The first industrial revolution (Industry 1.0) began with a mechanical loom (Deane, 2010). Newly introduced machines could significantly increase productivity compared to manpower-based manufacturing. In this era, machines were individually operated, and there were no control systems to incorporate the functions of individual machines. Moreover, it was difficult to supervise the overall processes in the manufacturing line. Therefore, local machines had individual HMIs to analyse individual machine status and processing data, which were not integrated between machines. The HMIs were not complicated in this era because machines provided simple functions, leading to limited information from the machine. These machines usually included mechanical input controls (e. g., lever and analogue dial) and small displays that provide machine status (Ivergard and Hunt, 2008). BI is a representative format for HMI in this era. BIs are non-interactive interfaces where users first need to enter all commands before batch processing and then receive the output when the processing is completed. Users cannot interrupt the batch processing until its completion. IBM 029 Card Punch is an example of the BI (IBM, 1964).

During the second industrial revolution (Industry 2.0), the electrified mass production system began, which enabled the supervision of data from the manufacturing line and controlled the integrated manufacturing process. In this era, the demand of HMIs considerably increased as they were necessary to supervise and control the system (Papcun et al., 2018). At the manufacturing site, an independent control room with integrated supervisory systems was adopted to systematically observe the overall manufacturing process in one place (Ivergard and Hunt, 2008). Therefore, the integrated systems included many functions and tasks. Moreover, the task and information complexity inevitably increased compared to the previous manufacturing context. To address the complexity, researchers started developing HMIs for performing tasks effectively and efficiently. Accordingly, CLI and TBI were actively used. The CLI was used to control the production process with a sequential set of commands and specific syntax. Punch cards and machine codes were the main input methods in CLI (Fierheller, 2006). As users of CLI had to learn cryptic commands to control sensors and devices, it required much learning effort. Compared to CLI, TBI eased the operation efforts as text-based commands could be programmed, saved, and reused (Ellis and Naffah, 1987). The commands became simple, similar to natural language, which eased the operators’ learning effort and cognitive load during use. Moreover, TBI reduced the operator’s extra effort by simplifying the machine output decoding tasks, thereby decreasing the operator’s cognitive load. Therefore, using the TBI was easier than using the BI and CLI technologies. However, TBI had limitations in presenting various types of information, such as images and graphs.

The third industrial revolution (Industry 3.0) is generally accepted as a digital revolution owing to the introduction of computerized robots and automation in manufacturing sites (Noyes and Bransby, 2001). With the introduction of automated and integrated systems, manufacturing systems had produced vast amounts of data. Consequently, electromechanical-based HMIs were limited to present information and control complicated systems. Accordingly, a technological shift from electromechanical HMIs to computer-based HMIs enabled graphical information to be presented, which increased the possibility of capturing more information from various functions (Henderson and Card, 1986). The computer-based HMI comprised many functions, tasks, and information, which increased the complexity compared to the previous industrial revolution (Noyes and Bransby, 2001). Consequently, researchers and interface designers began developing graphical interfaces.

GUI was used in HMIs to supervise automated production processes (Noyes and Bransby, 2001). These GUIs used process instrumentation diagrams that displayed the production operations information. Information of every phase of the production system could be easily traceable and manageable from remotely controlled HMIs (Astrom, 1985). Operators could easily control any device on the shopfloor using a programmable logic controller (PLC) and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems. Furthermore, human operators interact with industrial robots using speech recognition-based HMIs, and an industrial case of welding task using voice commands has been reported (Bugmann and Pires, 2005). HMIs for production systems were more advanced and could communicate with other advanced technologies remotely (Ivergard and Hunt, 2008). The advent of SCADA system in factories for supervision of shopfloor gives the advantage of pictorial presentation of shopfloor information compared to Industry 2.0 (Ivergard and Hunt, 2008). Therefore, using the GUI was easier than using the TBI in factories. However, GUI had limitations in presenting SCADA-based graphical information in mobile devices such as tablets, phones, etc.

The fourth industrial revolution seeks to overcome the physical limitations of manufacturing sites using CPPS. The CPPS is a production system that integrates all production elements and sub-systems, irrespective of their physical location, using a cyber-network (Vaidya et al.,

2018). A smart factory is a representative form of production in the era of Industry 4.0. As operators in smart factories require to supervise multiple shopfloors of production systems, HMIs started evolving accordingly. First, HMIs are equipped with IoT technologies and embedded network systems to support teleworking (Xu et al., 2014). As CPPS enables data collection from physical systems (e.g., field sensors and actuators) (Gorecky et al., 2014), there is no need to work at a designated site. Operators can observe the manufacturing process even if they are not present at the site (Lee et al., 2015). Additionally, the production process can be supervised simultaneously by different authorized users (e.g., operators, managers, and engineers) (Duman and Akdemir, 2021). Second, various interaction modalities (e.g., voice interactions) can be used. Tasks performed by an operator can vary based on the change in work using novel technologies, such as VR and AR. Consequently, efforts have been made to develop a natural user interface (NUI) that enables operators to use their naturalistic language, gestures, and body movements as input (Meixner et al., 2010). As this is developed based on naturalistic behaviors, learning efforts for NUI are much lower than those for other UIs. Furthermore, NUIs are expected to result in easier operations in CPPSs (Garcia et al., 2019; Monostori et al., 2016).

We found a paradigm shift in the manufacturing industry and in related HMIs. In each industrial revolution, the demand for HMIs has been increasing (e.g., data collection and management from factory facilities, communication between operators, etc.). Researchers and practitioners have attempted to develop new forms and features of HMIs to fulfil these requirements. With the latest intervention of manufacturing technologies (e.g., smart factories), HMIs in manufacturing sites must also be changed accordingly. For example, HMIs should support functions and tasks in smart factories, such as the supervision of multiple shopfloors and supporting teleworks. Accordingly, we found it is necessary to investigate HMIs and related matters, such as functions, tasks, and information type, to provide insight into the development of HMIs in smart factories.

## 3. Method

Among the various literature review strategies, we selected the SLR method to achieve the research objective and answer the research questions because it is a systematic and replicable approach (Booth et al., 2016). The SLR method is commonly understood as a powerful tool for evaluating published work (Booth et al., 2016; Cooper, 1998). We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) (Moher et al., 2009). Four stages are included in this approach: identification, screening, eligibility, and final inclusion. Fig. 2 illustrates the overall flow of the process.

## 3.1. Search and selection process

Identification Stage: In this stage, we conducted a search and collection of articles. Thirteen keywords were elicited from the research questions, and they were divided into three keyword groups: Group A, Group B, and Group C (see Table 1). A combination of three keywords from independent groups with the “AND” Boolean searched the articles from the databases. For example, keyword combinations, such as “Industry 4.0 + User interface + Human information processing,” “Industry 4.0 + User interface + Workload,” “Industry 4.0 +vUser interface + Human operator,” and “Industry 4.0 + User interface + Human error.” Consequently, 72 keyword combinations were used to collect articles (3 × 6 × 4 = 72). After applying all combinations, the discovered articles were gathered. Two thousand and sixty-five records (papers) were searched and gathered from all three databases (ScienceDirect: 1792; Web of Science: 60; IEEE Xplore: 213). The search and gathering process was conducted in December 2020.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 2. Flow diagram of systematic search and selection process.

Screening Stage The screening process was performed based on two steps in this stage. First, we deleted redundant records using “Mendeley” reference management software. amongst the 2065 articles, 515 records remained after removing duplicates. Then, we examined the titles and abstracts of the remaining articles with the following screening criteria: (1) articles that were not related to smart factory context, (2) articles that did not cover HMI issues and (3) articles that were purely technical, developmental, and electrical/mechanical/computer engineering relevant. After these two screening steps, 211 articles remained.

Eligibility Stage In this stage, we reviewed the full-text papers. One hundred and fifty articles that were not closely related to RQs were excluded. Sixty-one records were selected to answer the RQs.

Final Inclusion Stage While reviewing the articles, we traversed the references of the remaining 61 articles. We identified 16 articles that were not detected during the search process. These articles were included, and the final records were 77.

## 3.2. Data analysis strategy

To answer RQ1, we selected 30 articles based on a two-step process. First, we reviewed the full article and identified its relevance to RQ1. Second, we created a table for the definitions and description of functions, tasks, and information used in HMI in the context of the smart factory. To answer RQ2, we selected 32 articles using a two-step process. First, we reviewed the full article and identified articles relevant to the RQ2. In the review step, we identify different interaction modalities and their usage in smart factory operations. Second, we created a table for the definition and description of the interaction modality. Additionally, we describe the relationship between the task and interaction modalities in the smart factory context. To answer RQ3, we selected 15 papers based on keywords and reviewed the full paper. In the review step, we identify papers that reflect the knowledge of human factor issues in smart factories owing to HMI design. Accordingly, a table is presented along with a discussion to answer RQ3.

## 4. Results

4.1. Research question (RQ1): what types of functions, tasks, and information are used in smart factories?

We identified four types of functions that are widely mentioned in smart factories: operation and supervision (F1), management (F2), maintenance service (F3), and cybersecurity (F4) (Alc´acer and Cruz-- Machado, 2019; Cimini et al., 2020; Gorecky et al., 2014; Kannus and Ilvonen, 2018; Mourtzis and Vlachou, 2018; Siegert et al., 2020). Fig. 3 presents the smart factory functions, tasks, and information types that we found in the literature. In this paper, the functions of the smart factory are defined as departmental activities where workers perform tasks to accomplish their jobs. We identified that several tasks were executed to achieve functional objectives. Various information types are presented in HMIs when performing tasks. Table 2 lists the smart factory functions and their definitions.

Table 2 presents definitions of the four functions, which have been associated with seven tasks, each with their own subtasks. We defined seven main tasks to establish a relationship between tasks and functions. Table 3 presents the definitions of these seven tasks, and Table 4 pre-sents the tasks and subtasks. To understand the source of the information presented on the HMI, we need to discuss the tasks that are executed using the HMI for each smart factory function. The relationships between the functions, tasks, and information are explained below.

The first function in the smart factory is operation and supervision (F1). In this function, the operator oversees the activities of the production unit by performing several tasks such as monitoring, controlling machine parameters, machine scheduling, assembling, sharing reports with the production manager, and detecting alarms from a remote factory location (Cimini et al., 2020; Garcia et al., 2019; Gorecky et al., 2014; Kiangala and Wang, 2019; Wallhoff et al., 2007). Operators perform these tasks using various information types, such as machine parameters, sensor level, machine set points, operation data, machine programs and code, and start and restart commands (Table 4).

The second function in the smart factory is management (F2). Managers manage production systems and processes by performing several tasks, such as administrative tasks, resource scheduling, production sequencing, and planning (Adwernat et al., 2020; Belkadi et al., 2020; Longo et al., 2017; Mittelstadt ¨ et al., 2015; Wang, 2013). These tasks are performed using an HMI and various information types are processed, such as production reports, employee ID, machine ID, process plans, and updated and modified technical documents (e.g., notices, shopfloor procedure, component datasheet; see Table 4).

The third function in the smart factory is the maintenance service (F3), which deals with the repair and servicing of shopfloor equipment, such as machines, sensors, and systems, for a stable production process (Gorecky et al., 2014). Accordingly, engineers perform several tasks, such as machine testing, repairing, troubleshooting errors, report sharing, simulation, scheduling, and machine rescheduling (Gorecky et al., 2014; Longo et al., 2017). The information types presented on the HMI during the execution of these tasks include machine parameters, troubleshooting procedures, errors, and warning messages (Table 4).

The fourth function in the smart factory is cybersecurity (F4), which deals with the identification, management, and control of unauthorized data in the network cloud (Rubio et al., 2019). This function is vital in the manufacturing system to protect against threats and cyberattacks (Alcacer ´ and Cruz-Machado, 2019). The HMI device is well connected to the network cloud through IoTs and wireless embedded network systems. Accordingly, security executives can perform tasks such as authentication, security assessment, unauthorized data identification, network configuration, and node selection (Lezzi et al., 2018; O’Donovan et al., 2019). The types of information presented on the HMI during the execution of these tasks include network ID, node ID, user ID, WEP access code, machine ID, and authorization code. Table 4 lists the detailed associations of functions with task and information types.

## 4.2. Research question (RQ2): what interaction modalities are used for HMI in smart factories?

In a smart factory, an HMI interaction modality is a type of input and output method for interacting with interfaces using the human senses. Interaction is a key feature of HMIs because it facilitates the use of the HMI. We identified five interaction modalities that are used to perform tasks in smart factories: gaze, voice, tactile, gesture, and haptic interactions. To better understand these interaction modalities, we define and explain each of them in Table 5 and the subsequent paragraphs.

Gaze interaction uses eye-related data as an input to interact with the machine interface. For input actions, eye parameters such as eye fixation, saccades, and eye blinks are used to operate HMIs (Wallhoff et al., 2007). These parameters are measured by an eye-tracking system that transmits signals to the machine interface for appropriate gaze inputs (Jaimes and Sebe, 2007). Operators use gaze interaction to perform shop-floor monitoring and control tasks (Moniri et al., 2016). For example, the operator performs a virtual production task, including identification and selection of objects in a virtual smart factory environment (Wallhoff et al., 2007). This type of interaction modality requires proper eye control and precision for task execution.

Voice interaction uses voice commands as inputs to operate HMIs in a smart factory (Gorecky et al., 2014). Such interactions require a strong voice recognition algorithm and a knowledge resource database to process coded voice commands (Longo et al., 2017). Voice interaction requires a record of the operator’s voice samples to authenticate the operator and a set of voice commands for monitoring, controlling, scheduling, and maintaining a smart factory (Weimer and Ganapathy, 1989). For example, an operator performed a maintenance task to detect machine failure and performed a machine reset procedure using a developed voice-enabled assistant (Longo and Padovano, 2020). This type of interaction modality requires that a specific set of commands or keywords be memorized by the operator to execute tasks.

Gesture interaction uses hand, finger, and head movements to operate the HMI (De Pace et al., 2020). Gesture interaction requires a record of the operator’s hand movement samples to identify the commands to perform monitoring, controlling, assembling, scheduling, and maintenance tasks in a smart factory (Meixner et al., 2010; Weimer and Ganapathy, 1989). A human operator can initiate and control industrial robots via specific hand and finger movements (Ahmed et al., 2019). The smart factory operator uses different hand gestures, such as pointing a finger or grabbing, to control the machine parameters (Meixner et al.,

2010). This type of interaction modality requires appropriate hand control and precision for task execution.

Tactile interaction is a touch-based method that provides input to the HMI. This interaction requires physical contact with the interface screen to monitor, control, schedule, assemble, and perform maintenance tasks (Gorecky et al., 2014; Schmitt et al., 2013). For example, an operator used tactile interaction to control the flow unit in a smart factory (Schmitt et al., 2013). Gorecky et al. (2014) used a tablet-based HMI for tactile interaction to control and maintain a smart production system. This type of interaction modality demands focused attention to simultaneously observe both virtual and physical objects.

Haptic interaction can create an experience of touch by conveying forces, vibrations, temperature, or motions to the operator. A wearable haptic glove connects with the HMI to perform monitoring and control tasks. Haptic interaction can be used along with other interaction modalities, such as voice and gestures (Ahmed et al., 2019). For example, an operator can use haptic interaction and voice interaction to perform assembly tasks. In the assembly task, the operator used the ring and index fingers to receive haptic responses for the error output (Funk et al., 2016). This type of interaction modality requires extra effort on the part of the operator to learn specific sensations (as input/machine feedback) to perform specific tasks (Krupitzer et al., 2020). Operators need to be quick and sensitive to touch so that no input responses from the machine are overlooked.

## 4.3. Research question (RQ3): how does the system and HMI impact human operators in a smart factory?

We identified how information and interaction impact human operators from cognitive and physical perspectives. With the advent of novel technologies for smart factory operations, such as human–robot collaboration and AR/VR-based HMIs, operators require extra training to learn these technologies to better perform tasks. These technologies require both cognitive and physical abilities to perform tasks (Malik and Bilberg, 2019). However, the operator’s cognitive abilities are more important than their physical abilities in a smart factory. In the previous industrial revolution, operators had to move around the factory and perform more physical activities (Noyes and Bransby, 2001; Papcun et al., 2018). However, because the machines are connected in smart factories, operators can easily supervise the production process from one place using the HMI. The use of automated machines in smart factory functions and machines connected with HMIs using IoT can provide an enormous amount of machine information to the operator in real time, thereby increasing the operator’s cognitive workload (Wittenberg, 2015). We also found that the information presentation methods (e.g., 2-dimensional images, 3-dimensional images, and video) and vast amount of information presented on the HMI create visual complexity, leading to cognitive load on the operator (Kiangala and Wang, 2019). We found that the cognitive load, fatigue, and decrease in operator attention are caused by complex tasks and decisions that are required in critical scenarios in digital factories (Tsutsumi et al., 2020). Additionally, performing excessive cognitive tasks using the HMI can increase the chances of human error and decrease the operator’s performance (Wittenberg, 2015). The RQ3 results presented in Table 6 show the cognitive and physical factors that impact the operator due to the information type and interaction modalities.

## 5. Discussion

In this systematic literature review, our goal was to understand the tasks, information, and interaction modalities of HMIs in smart factory functions. We also investigated the impact of information and interaction modalities on human operators. This paper explains the evolution of the HMI in different industrial revolutions and discusses studies on various HMI types. Based on the literature review, we proposed a conceptual research framework and developed three research questions. The results of the three research questions are discussed in the following subsections.

## 5.1. Functions, tasks, and information in the smart factory

In a smart factory production system, functions are departmental activities where humans perform tasks to accomplish their jobs using HMIs. As shown in Fig. 3, the HMIs of a smart factory are widely used for four functions: operations and supervision, management, maintenance, and cybersecurity. Researchers have individually reported these four functions using HMIs from a smart factory perspective (Alcacer ´ and Cruz-Machado, 2019; Krupitzer et al., 2020; Meixner et al., 2010). However, we exempt the identification of tasks and information types and consider these functions concurrently.

In the previous industrial revolutions, factory functions were performed by completing various tasks that were not traceable from a single device or machine, and functions were also not well connected with each other. There were no interoperable functions, and real-time data collection and control were possible for only a few functions (Noyes and Bransby, 2001). For example, operation and supervision functions in previous industrial sites gathered real-time shopfloor data and sensor/machine data from monitoring and controlling tasks using PLC and SCADA systems. However, real-time data acquisition from tasks such as monitoring, controlling, report sharing, alarm detection, scheduling, and task rescheduling was not feasible concurrently. Similarly, other functions, such as management, maintenance, and cybersecurity, were not interconnected and could not share real-time data.

Table 3 Tasks and definitions.

| Tasks | Definitions |
| --- | --- |
| Monitoring task | The monitoring task is defined as the observation of the production system, process, or machine with the help of an HMI. |
| Controlling task | The controlling task is defined as maintaining process parameters in a stable range and maintaining stable shopfloor operation based on a threshold. |
| Assembling task | The assembling task is defined as identifying and combining different parts of the manufacturing products or machines. |
| Scheduling of machine | The scheduling of machine task is defined as setting up the machine operation parameters and uploading programs to achieve better production performance. |
| Scheduling of workforce and operations | The scheduling of workforce and operations task is defined as assigning jobs to workers, managing manpower for shopfloor operations, and setting up operational procedures for the shopfloor. |
| Maintenance and repair task | The maintenance task is defined as repair and upkeep of production machines used in industrial settings and troubleshooting machine or system errors. |
| Administrative task | The administrative task is defined as managing jobs, the production system, machines, manpower, and creating technical and non-technical documents. |

Table 2 presents the definitions and contexts for smart factory functions. In F1 of the smart factory, departmental responsibilities are different from the previous industrial revolution. F1 activities include supervision of factory instrumentation systems using IoT-based networked clouds, automated production time allocation for users and machine jobs, online report sharing with production managers, robotbased alarms and shopfloor management systems (Cimini et al., 2020). Operators, engineers, and production supervisors primarily conduct these activities (Holm, 2018). HMIs are used by all these users for various tasks, and the information is managed through cloud computing. Departmental responsibilities also change in F2, due to the advent of smart management applications and network cloud-based management solutions that can operate on multiplatform software and hardware. These applications and online solutions are incorporated into dedicated smart factory HMIs (Longo et al., 2017). F2 activities include online production planning, real-time analysis of production data, and online sharing of production jobs and assignments for operators and management teams using HMI applications. | Voice interaction | A meaningful set of voice commands as an input to interact with a machine interface. | (Longo and Padovano, 2020) |
| Gesture interaction | Expressive and meaningful body motion (fingers, hand, head, etc.) with the intent of interacting with a machine interface. | (Garcia et al., 2019) |
| Tactile interaction | Physical contact with the surface of the machine interface with the intent to perform an action. | (Carter and Fourney, 2005) |
| Haptic interaction | The technology that encompasses touch feedback or other bodily sensations to perform actions. | (Carter and Fourney, 2005) |

members (Longo et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2013). Maintenance engineers are equipped with the latest hardware and software to perform repair and troubleshooting tasks (Gorecky et al., 2014). F3 combines information obtained from different functions for predictive maintenance using advanced prediction models and analytical tools (Alcacer ´ and Cruz-Machado, 2019; Gorecky et al., 2014). For example, F3 couples F1 information (such as machine/sensor data and operation data) and F2 information (machine run time and machine shutdown time) to predict the best maintenance model and repair the machine or system. In F4 of the smart factory, departmental responsibilities include securing the shopfloor, production, operation, and management data for the smart factory. HMIs are also used to verify user identity and block unauthorized access to the smart factory’s networked cloud (Lezzi et al., 2018). The smart factory security system operates on two computing systems: cloud computing (i.e., centralized) and fog computing (decentralized), both of which are used to deliver real-time embedded machine learning engineering applications (O’Donovan et al., 2019).

Table 3 defines the tasks, and Table 4 presents the relationships between the functions, tasks, and information types. Table 4 reveals that smart factory functions have 18 tasks, including subtasks, and the execution of these tasks presents various types of information on the HMI. For example, Meixner et al. (2010) reported a practical case of HMI use in a smart factory. They developed a UPC 450 prototype (a wireless and touch screen HMI) that presents information such as machine, operation, and production data to execute monitoring and control tasks. In F2, Longo et al. (2017) developed a voice-enabled HMI that presented information, such as production reports and technical and non-technical documents, for the operator to execute administrative tasks (entering production data into the factory cloud). In F3, for example, the UPC 450 HMI presented information to operators, including machine parameters, troubleshooting procedures, and error messages, to execute error detection, troubleshooting, and repairing tasks (Meixner et al., 2010). In this context, we determined that operators need to process complex information during these tasks, and that the operator requires rigorous maintenance training to learn how to use the HMI. Gorecky et al. (2014)

reported that the operator moved from one location to another to perform repair and troubleshooting tasks in F3. Information presented on the HMI showed troubleshooting procedures, errors, and warning messages. In F4, security-related information regarding the smart factory production process, machines, and systems is a major concern (Lezzi et al., 2018). Thus, tasks such as authentication, security assessment, unauthorized data identification, network configuration, and node selection must be performed on a secure server (O’Donovan et al., 2019). We found that operators dealt with critical information in a cloud network server using an HMI. Therefore, information security becomes important when performing tasks using an HMI in F4.

## 5.2. HMI interaction modalities in the smart factory

Table 5 lists five interaction modalities and their basic definitions—gaze, voice, gesture, tactile, and haptic interactions—which are widely used in smart factory HMIs. We found that the use of interaction modalities in HMIs depends on the different tasks of the smart factory functions.

Gaze interaction uses eye blinks, eye fixation, and saccades to interact with HMIs. These parameters are decoded by HMI applications to execute monitoring tasks (Moniri et al., 2016). Jaimes and Sebe (2007) reported that gaze interaction can be used to quickly identify an object on an HMI screen. Wallhoff et al. (2007) used eye fixation data inputs to select 3D objects (sphere, cone, etc.) to perform a virtual production line sorting task.

Voice interaction is actively used to perform maintenance tasks. For example, Weimer and Ganpathy (1989) used voice commands for navigation in virtual control panel screens. We found that voice interaction is an efficient way to search and control machine parameters, because it allows users to access much information and use voice keywords to monitor and control tasks.

Gesture interaction uses hand and finger movements to interact with an HMI (Gracia et al., 2019). Weimer and Ganpathy (1989) reported hand movement decoding to select buttons on a virtual control panel, where the operator selected geometric features. Wallhoff et al. (2007) also utilized hand gesture inputs to move, grab, and dispose of 3D objects (sphere, cone, etc.) in assembly tasks in a production line. Gesture interactions are widely used in control, maintenance, and assembly tasks in smart factories because they enable operators to naturally interact with machines (Gorecky et al., 2014; Malik and Bilberg, 2019; Wallhoff et al., 2007). We found that hand gesture interaction could also perform tasks quickly using micro-interactions, such as holding an object, moving an object, selecting a button, and zooming in or out, especially in AR contexts (Hietanen et al., 2020).

Tactile interaction involves the sense of touch (Carter and Fourney, 2005), and is mostly used for monitoring, controlling, maintenance, assembling, scheduling, and administrative tasks (Gorecky et al., 2014). The operator performs these tasks using HMI applications that are incorporated in mobile phones and tablets (Schmitt et al., 2013). We found that tactile interaction was widely used for most tasks, as shown in Table 3. Several tactile micro-interactions, such as single tap, double tap, scroll up/down, zoom-in/-out and swipe left/right (Hinckley and Sinclair, 1999), exist in HMIs to execute operations in smart factories. Tactile interactions are closely associated with haptic interactions. In several cases, tactile and haptic interactions are used together to perform tasks (Carter and Fourney, 2005).

Haptics is related to the sense of touch (Carter and Fourney, 2005) and is a form of nonverbal communication (sound, vibration, touch, and temperature). In HMIs, haptic interaction is provided by wearable devices that produce specific sensations (output responses from the HMI) to the operator while performing monitoring and controlling tasks using the HMI (Tannous et al., 2020). A wearable glove was provided to an operator for haptic interaction while performing an assembly task. The operator’s ring and index fingers were used to receive the error output (vibration as a haptic response) from the machine during the assembly task (Funk et al., 2016). We found that haptic interaction is widely used for monitoring and controlling tasks. Task performance varies depending on how quickly operators feel specific sensations and take appropriate actions. Therefore, haptic interaction requires operators to understand the exact working mechanisms (e.g., haptic feedback).

## 5.3. Effects of smart factory systems and HMIs on operators in the smart factory

We found that the human operators were affected cognitively and physically by the smart factory systems and HMIs. We summarized each article and identified the reasons for these impacts on human operators in smart factories (Table 6).

In smart factories, the task performance of a human operator can be physically and cognitively affected. The physical aspect of the human operator concerns how the human body responds to physical work demands, whereas the cognitive aspect of the human operator concerns the mental demands required for smart factory tasks. The smart factory has several tasks that can affect the human operator physically and cognitively while using an HMI. During task execution, the human operator’s head, hands, fingers, neck, spine, and posture can be affected. Similarly, the human operator is cognitively affected by complex and difficult tasks, which lead to increased mental workload, stress, and perceptual load.

We found that operators could be physically affected by physical tasks (e.g., assembly tasks). For example, Bortolini et al. (2020) developed a motion analysis system for the digitalization of the human body and analysed human body postures while executing assembly tasks within industrial workstations. They reported that the human operator had a risk of musculoskeletal disorder while performing an assembly task in an AR-based production system. Poor and Jude (2019) have also reported that when executing a maintenance task, the operator must stand and hold the HMI device at a fixed height for a long time, which can cause back pain and strain on the hand muscles. The use of advanced technologies, such as human–robot interaction, can be another issue. We observed that human–robot interaction while executing tasks on the shopfloor creates safety-related issues for human operators. For example, Kadir et al. (2019) reported a risk of collision between operators and robots while collaborating to perform maintenance tasks on the shopfloor. Moreover, operators experienced physical burdens on the head and neck due to the unbalanced centre of mass created by the VR/AR devices. They also reported that assembly instructions presented on an AR holographic screen created difficulties for the operator in processing accurate information during the task because of the limited field of view (Danielsson et al., 2020).

A large amount of information should be processed when operators use HMIs in smart factories. Table 4 depicts the various information types that a human operator uses to perform several tasks. We found that human operators had difficulty performing searching tasks due to the large volume of information. For example, Queshmy et al. (2019) reported that human error occurs in the production line because of five factors: thinking, looking, counting, information searching, and deciding, all of which affect the mental workload of the operator. There are also two additional factors—the amount of information and the information presentation method in a complex task—that can create a mental workload on operators, thereby affecting their performance (Mittelstadt ¨ et al., 2015). Ansari et al. (2020) also reported two cognitive stress factors for the operator in assembling tasks: the complexity of the product parts being assembled and the complexity of the smart factory environment. From the SLR, we found that tasks, information types, and interaction modalities play vital roles in human performance. In future smart factories, the physical and cognitive aspects of human operators must be considered when designing HMIs for better performance and safety of the human operator.

## 5.4. HMI design recommendation and challenges

Interface designers can consider factors derived from our research review, such as smart factory functions, types of tasks, information types, and interaction modality types, in designing efficient interfaces. Additionally, they can refer to the context in which the HMI is used, as mentioned in Section 4 (Tables 4 and 6). Our study can help interface designers understand user needs and requirements for designing HMIs from the smart factory functions, tasks, information, and interaction perspectives. In addition, we discussed the advantages and disadvantages of the interaction types along with the tasks. Interface designers can plan screen layouts based on smart factory functions, as mentioned in Section 4.1. In the future, designing HMIs will be challenging because interface designers need to understand auditory and visual information complexity in the HMI, task complexity, the critical use scenario, smart factory functionality, and multimodality interactions (Thomessen, 2012). We also recommend that HMI designers consider both the physical and cognitive aspects in different smart factory scenarios. Overall, interface designers require an operator-focused HMI design methodology from a smart factory perspective. We recommend that users first undergo training and learn interaction modalities to increase the relevant cognitive load for better performance. Users should have updated mental models for information presentation methods and task novelty.

The challenges associated with HMIs in smart factory operations are as follows: (a) they require a strong cybersecurity network to protect the factory cloud from unauthorized users (Lezzi et al., 2018), (b) human-centred technology is necessary to improve the usability of the HMI (Malik and Bilberg, 2019), and (c) guidelines for smart factory HMI design must be formulated from cognitive and physical perspectives.

## 5.5. Economic, social, and environmental advantages of using HMI in smart factory

In Industry 3.0-based factories, there are separate control consoles for many machines and computer-based display systems (SCADA systems), which are very expensive and bulky. Moreover, these systems require a team of operators to supervise production operations, which increases expenses (Noyes and Bransby, 2001). The advantages of using a single HMI for supervising multiple smart factories are as follows: (a) it reduces the hardware expenses by replacing large control panels, machine displays, and a PC-based supervision system; (b) it reduces the expenses and requirement for additional operators to supervise the shopfloor, because a single operator can supervise multiple shopfloors anywhere and anytime using network cloud computing technology; (c) an HMI can detect system errors easily and can maintain the system efficiently using a past data feed and intelligent predictive maintenance model; it can, therefore, design an appropriate maintenance plan for businesses; (d) data availability and interoperability through the HMI software enables the development of an efficient production system that reduces expenses and extra workload on humans, thereby increasing the smart factory productivity. The production efficiency of a smart factory can be improved using HMI-based systems, which will eventually improve the economic conditions of the manufacturing industry.

The social advantages of HMI use in smart factories include mobility, work flexibility, and safety. Factory people can work from home and manage their work shifts easily by logging into the HMI software from anywhere. In addition, HMI use provides secure interaction with machines in shopfloor operations. HMIs allow operators to work with heavy electrical and thermal machines in a hazardous workspace from a safe distance and protect factory people from harmful gasses and workplace noise. HMIs can inform the appropriate factory people about critical production system situations by sending emergency messages and maintaining safety in smart factories. Therefore, HMI use is beneficial for factory workers’ social life and safety, which eventually enhances smart factory productivity.

The environmental advantages of using HMIs are that they require a small area setup, leads to less power consumption, and reduces waste and the risk of a noisy environment. HMIs in smart factories replace heavy control consoles that occupy large spaces in factory areas. Eventually, this can help save space for nature and human beings to live. In Industry 3.0, the control consoles used large wires for communication between machines and humans. Wireless HMIs replace wire-based control consoles used for short- and long-distance communication, which reduces the volume of wire waste created by factories every year. HMIs also reduce the amount of power consumed by heavy control consoles. In addition, control consoles attached to machines create a noisy working environment for factory people. HMIs decrease the risk of working in noisy environments. Hence, the use of HMIs in smart factories is very beneficial for the production system and the factory workers.

## 6. Conclusions

In this study, we conducted a systematic literature review to understand the HMI in smart factories. We elicited the smart factory functions to identify the tasks, types of information, and interaction types and described how these systems and HMIs impact human operators. Our work contributes to providing domain knowledge and understanding of HMIs in a smart factory. In particular, the detailed contributions of this study are as follows: (a) identified information types, tasks, and interactions of HMI in smart factory functions, (b) identified the impact of HMI on human operators, (c) provided recommendations and suggestions to the interface designer and for HMI users.

The current study has the following limitations that should be considered in future studies: (a) We applied a systematic keyword search process using only three major databases to identify studies related to our research questions; however, there is a possibility that some articles from other databases were missed, (b) We applied a systematic literature review method and not a meta-review approach. Future studies with a meta-review approach can provide a deeper understanding of this topic.

Naveen Kumar is a Postdoctoral Associate in the Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering at Gyeongsang National University. His-research interests lie on Human-Computer Interaction, User Experience Design, Cognitive Ergonomics, and Industry 4.0.

Seul Chan Lee is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering at Gyeongsang National University. His-research goal is to make systems and devices better based on the theories and methodologies of Human Factors and Human-Computer Interaction, especially in the fields of autonomous vehicle, VR/AR, smart factory.
